Amplitude measurements serve as a primary method for detecting new physics beyond the Standard Model. This work introduces a statistical framework designed to quantify the experimental significance of such discoveries, explicitly accounting for systematic uncertainties. We define a novel metric termed "effective significance," which synthesizes both statistical evidence and the precision of a measured amplitude. This metric is particularly vital for searches targeting new phenomena where a null result still yields meaningful constraints on theoretical models. We illustrate the methodology through applications to LHC searches for heavy resonances decaying into diphotons and dileptons, as well as a study of electron electric dipole moments.

We introduce a new, general framework designed to model the dynamical evolution of gamma-ray burst (GRB) afterglows. This approach integrates the standard self-similar solutions with a broad spectrum of non-self-similar solutions, enabling the analysis of diverse physical scenarios. Within this model, we examine the afterglow behavior across varying internal and external conditions, including the transition from relativistic to sub-relativistic phases. We demonstrate that the framework successfully reproduces the temporal evolution of afterglows in both uniform and structured media, covering cases with and without jet effects. Furthermore, we apply this model to the afterglow of GRB 110215A, showing that it accurately accounts for the observed data. Finally, we propose that this novel framework serves as a robust tool for investigating the afterglow dynamics of other GRBs.

This paper investigates the problem of partitioning the vertex set of a bipartite graph $G$ into two subsets, $A$ and $B$, such that the induced subgraphs $G[A]$ and $G[B]$ are both $k$-colorable. We establish that for any bipartite graph $G$ with maximum degree $\Delta$, there exists a partition satisfying this $k$-colorability condition whenever $k \geq \Delta - \log_2(\Delta - 1) + 1$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bound is tight for all $k \geq 3$. The result represents an improvement over the prior bound of $k \geq \Delta - \sqrt{\Delta} + 2$, which was introduced by Kierstead and Trotter in 1991. Finally, we present a polynomial-time algorithm with a running time of $O(n \cdot 2^{\Delta})$ to compute such a partition.

Bipedal locomotion is a primary focus of robotics research, yet current models often lack the efficiency and resilience required for real-world applications. This study proposes a propulsion-assisted framework designed to enhance both efficiency and resilience in bipedal systems. We introduce a new propulsion model that incorporates a foot-fixed propulsion frame, enabling the generation of propulsion forces relative to the foot. This approach allows for the creation of a propulsion-assisted gait, where the propulsion phase is treated as a distinct movement segment. We define a unified optimization problem that simultaneously determines the gait and propulsion profiles, utilizing a novel cost function that accounts for the energy required to generate propulsion forces. Simulation results demonstrate that this propulsion-assisted gait achieves a 10% reduction in metabolic energy compared to standard gaits. Furthermore, simulations of ground reaction force disturbances confirm that the added propulsion capability significantly improves the system's resilience.

A complete residue map for a field extension $K/k$ is defined as a function $f$ that maps all elements of $K$ to $k$ while satisfying the property that $f(xy) = f(x)f(y)$ for any $x, y$ in $k$. This paper demonstrates the existence of complete residue maps for several well-known extensions, including the $p$-adic numbers over the rational field, the field of rational functions over the field of constants, and the cyclotomic extension of the $p$-adic numbers over the field of $p$-adic numbers.

This paper introduces HyperDegrade, a novel technique designed to accelerate hyperthreading-based DoS attacks by degrading the performance of competing threads on multi-threaded CPUs. While prior research has focused on single-threaded attacks, this study demonstrates that the presence of a thread can significantly impair the execution of others sharing the same physical core. HyperDegrade leverages this phenomenon by strategically injecting threads that introduce cache pollution and artificial latency, thereby reducing the target thread's throughput. The authors present a comprehensive evaluation across diverse workloads and hardware platforms, confirming the method's efficacy. Furthermore, they developed an automated tool for deploying HyperDegrade attacks. The results indicate that this approach can achieve up to a 1000-fold performance reduction in victim threads, with a 1000x increase in efficiency compared to existing methods.

This paper introduces a new unknotting procedure applicable to both traditional and welded links. The authors establish that the minimal number of moves required to unknot a link within this framework is precisely the unknotting number for traditional links and the welded unknotting number for welded links. Furthermore, the study examines the relationship between this novel procedure and other known unknotting techniques.

This paper demonstrates that the Fox-Hatcher loop, a well-known element within the third relative homotopy group of the group of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of the disk ($Diff^+_1(D^2)$), possesses a non-trivial Vassiliev characteristic of order three when evaluated on $Diff^+_1(D^2)$. This finding is significant because it represents the first time a non-trivial Vassiliev characteristic of order three has been identified for this specific group.

This study introduces a novel multi-agent framework designed to enhance the coordination of conventional robots through the strategic deployment of multiple agents. Within this system, each agent operates with restricted computational and communication capabilities, functioning as a specialized supervisor for a specific subset of robots. The primary objective is to optimize the collective performance of the robot fleet by strategically assigning agents to the robots. To achieve this, the paper formulates the problem as a non-convex optimization task and derives a closed-form solution for the associated cost function. Furthermore, it establishes a rigorous mathematical proof demonstrating that the proposed assignment strategy yields a 2-approximate solution relative to the optimal outcome. The practical viability of this approach is validated through a simulation environment featuring a multi-robot system tasked with navigating a complex, obstacle-filled environment.

Vertical federated learning (VFL) offers a promising approach for collaborative model training across organizations that partition data horizontally, effectively addressing privacy concerns while maintaining data locality. However, this method remains vulnerable to privacy attacks, particularly those targeting the inference stage where a malicious participant attempts to reconstruct private inputs from a benign counterpart using the trained model and its outputs. Existing defenses typically rely on adding noise to the model or the data, yet these strategies often degrade model performance or fail to provide robust protection. This paper introduces Pragmatic Privacy Assaults (PPA), a novel attack framework designed to reconstruct private data from the inference phase of VFL. Unlike prior methods, PPA operates without access to the model architecture, training data, or training labels, relying solely on the model's predictions. By employing a generative adversarial network (GAN) to generate synthetic data distributions that mimic the benign party's true dataset, PPA achieves high reconstruction accuracy. Extensive evaluations on both real-world and synthetic benchmarks demonstrate that PPA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in terms of data recovery precision.

Kernel methods are widely recognized for their effectiveness in classification and regression tasks, yet they often require selecting a kernel parameter that is not easily determined. This study introduces a novel, data-driven approach to estimating this parameter by leveraging pseudo-random Fourier features. The proposed estimator is designed to be consistent and offers a specific rate of convergence. Furthermore, we present a practical algorithm for determining the optimal parameter value. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through both synthetic experiments and real-world applications.

This paper introduces a novel Cartesian decomposition for the class of Garland products, extending the existing Cartesian decomposition of Heisenberg groups. Utilizing this new structure, we establish that the groups $G(\Gamma,\lambda)$ are non-isomorphic whenever the underlying graphs $\Gamma$ are non-isomorphic, provided the edge weight function $\lambda$ is sufficiently large. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Garland product $G(\Gamma,\lambda)$ admits a Carnot-Carath\'eodory metric if and only if $\lambda$ is large enough.

This paper examines the conditions under which a compact hypersurface $M$ embedded in the Euclidean space $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ can be conformally transformed into a surface with constant M\"obius scalar curvature. We establish that if a compact hypersurface $M$ in $\mathbb{S}^{n+1}$ possesses a conformally smooth structure and its M\"obius scalar curvature $R$ satisfies the inequality $R \geq n(n+1)$, then $M$ must be conformally equivalent to the standard sphere $\mathbb{S}^n$ equipped with its canonical metric. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the threshold $n(n+1)$ is sharp; specifically, if $R \geq n(n+1)-\epsilon$ for some $\epsilon > 0$, there exist compact hypersurfaces $M$ with conformally smooth structures that are not conformally equivalent to $\mathbb{S}^n$.

This study investigates resource allocation for simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) within a multi-service context. The framework considers a base station (BS) serving both an information receiver (IR) and an energy harvesting receiver (ER) via the same radio resources. The objective is to maximize the ER's harvested energy while satisfying the minimum data rate requirement of the IR. We examine two distinct power splitting (PS) strategies: a fixed PS ratio and an optimized PS ratio. For the fixed PS case, the problem is convex and solved directly. Conversely, the optimized PS scenario yields a non-convex problem addressed via successive convex approximation (SCA). Numerical simulations confirm that the proposed schemes outperform existing methods. Furthermore, results indicate that maximizing harvested energy is best achieved by prioritizing power allocation to the ER.

This study examines the distribution of avalanche sizes within the sandpile model defined on a Cayley graph of a finite group $G$, utilizing the group's generators to facilitate chip movement. We demonstrate that for an extensive class of groups, the resulting avalanche size distribution adheres to a power law with an exponent of approximately 0.45 across all system scales. Furthermore, we establish that the typical avalanche size grows logarithmically relative to the total number of elements in the group $G$.

The sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors is frequently constrained by the low-frequency response of their optical sensors. Enhancing this response typically requires injecting radiation pressure noise, a method that simultaneously elevates the detector's high-frequency response. This study introduces a novel approach to boost the low-frequency response using a Sagnac interferometer configured with a sloshing light path. This addition creates a position-dependent phase shift that mimics the radiation pressure noise effect on the primary interferometer. Crucially, this configuration ensures that the induced high-frequency response noise remains localized within the Sagnac loop, preventing it from contaminating the main detection channel.

This study examines an XL-MIMO stochastic access protocol designed for a single-user, multi-access scenario within a large-scale system. In this protocol, a base station equipped with a vast array of antennas serves a single user, who periodically transmits a packet containing both data and a unique identifier. The base station must identify the user based on this ID, a process known as non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). The identification relies on the distinct visibility patterns of the user's transmit antennas; specifically, the system detects which antennas can receive the packet. The paper derives the probability distribution of the number of visible antennas and the count of intersecting visibility areas. Furthermore, it analyzes the impact of these non-intersecting visibility areas on the overall identification success rate. The findings indicate that the number of visible antennas and intersecting visibility areas are influenced by the user's location, the antenna array's dimensions, and the packet's transmission angle. Finally, the study explores the relationship between the number of visible antennas and the packet's transmission angle.

This study investigates the observational signatures of substructures within protoplanetary disks disrupted by Vertical Shear Instability (VSI). We employ hydrodynamic simulations to examine how VSI-driven gaps influence both the gas and dust components across a range of disk parameters. Our findings indicate that VSI creates a broad annular gap in the gas surface density, extending from the pressure bump located at the outer edge of the pressure bump to the outer edge of the pressure bump. This gap is accompanied by a sharp, inward-facing pressure bump at its inner boundary, which serves to confine the inner disk. Regarding dust dynamics, we observe a significant reduction in the mid-infrared flux due to dust settling within the VSI gap, while the outer disk exhibits a distinct spiral pattern in the continuum emission. These structural features are robust across various disk models and remain largely unaffected by the presence of pressure bumps. Consequently, we predict that future high-resolution observations using ALMA and the ngVLA will be able to detect these characteristic gap-gap and spiral patterns, thereby confirming the presence of VSI activity.

The "Big Apple" represents a unique, high-energy event where a massive asteroid struck the surface of the Moon, creating a crater approximately 15 kilometers in diameter. This impact was so forceful that it ejected debris far beyond the lunar surface, allowing it to reach Earth and form a distinct crater on the planet's surface. The significance of this occurrence lies in its ability to provide valuable insights into the history of celestial bodies, the nature of cosmic impacts, and the evolution of our solar system. By studying the "Big Apple," researchers can better understand how such events shape planetary surfaces and contribute to our knowledge of astronomical processes.

This study introduces a frequency-resilient $\sqrt{\text{MS}}$ gate for two trapped ions, designed to function effectively even when there are mismatches in the trap frequencies of the ions' motional modes. By utilizing a balanced input state across multiple motional modes, this gate achieves high fidelity despite such imperfections. The approach is applicable to various two-qubit architectures, including those based on photons, superconducting circuits, and neutral atoms. Furthermore, the concept of input-state balancing is generalized to create a robust protocol for generating $\sqrt{\text{MS}}$ gates that remain resilient to frequency mismatches in any arbitrary number of motional modes.

This study introduces a new class of crystalline materials featuring a strongly linked Dirac cone, where the two components of the conduction band's spinor are tightly entangled. This unique property ensures that the conduction electrons maintain a robust spin-1/2 character while exhibiting a robustly suppressed Hall effect. Our theoretical framework predicts this exotic phase within the $4d$ transition metal family, specifically within the hexagonal arsenic-based crystals of Platinum (Pt) and Iridium (Ir). We anticipate that this novel phase can be experimentally verified through high-resolution ARPES measurements, which would reveal a single Dirac point per Brillouin zone accompanied by a distinctive, suppressed Hall response.

The potential discovery of a heavy neutral lepton (HNL) with a mass below approximately 1 GeV would significantly advance our understanding of neutrino physics. This paper outlines the anticipated sensitivity of the NA62 experiment at CERN to detect such an HNL via the decay channel $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. The study focuses on HNLs that decay within the detector volume, specifically targeting the decay mode $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N \to \pi^0 e^+ \ell^+ \ell^-$. By analyzing the projected background levels and the expected signal statistics, the authors establish a reach for the squared mixing element $|U_{eN}|^2$ as a function of the HNL mass $m_N$. The results indicate that NA62 will achieve a sensitivity of $|U_{eN}|^2 \approx 10^{-7}$ for HNL masses between 100 and 200 MeV, a range where the HNL is anticipated to decay inside the spectrometer.

Neural language models have largely superseded traditional $N$-gram approaches for generating text due to their superior ability to capture long-range linguistic dependencies. However, this shift comes with a drawback: neural models often produce text that sounds less natural than that generated by $N$-grams, a phenomenon we attribute to the fact that while $N$-grams excel at modeling local word sequences, neural networks tend to overlook these short-term dependencies. To address this, we propose a hybrid framework that integrates an $N$-gram linguistic model as a residual component within a neural architecture. Our experiments demonstrate that this combined approach significantly enhances the naturalness of generated text compared to using a neural model alone, achieving performance that rivals or even surpasses that of a standalone $N$-gram system.

Accurate 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction are essential for numerous computer vision applications. However, existing methods often struggle with robustness when encountering variations in pose, illumination, and occlusion. To address these challenges, we introduce Self-aligned Dual Facial Regression Networks (SADRNet), a novel framework designed for 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction. This approach integrates a dual-stage strategy: initially, a coarse alignment module estimates the 3D facial shape and camera pose, while subsequently, a fine alignment module refines the dense facial landmarks based on the prior estimates. Crucially, our self-alignment mechanism iteratively refines both the landmark positions and the 3D shape parameters to ensure precise fitting. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SADRNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in 3D dense face alignment and reconstruction across multiple datasets.

This study investigates the impact of stochastic and quantum fluctuations on inflation within the $\alpha$-attractor framework, specifically analyzing scenarios where these disturbances trigger Primordial Black Hole (PBH) formation. We examine both an additional monomial term in the potential and the influence of a running spectral index. Our findings indicate that PBHs can form in this model under specific conditions regarding the potential's shape and the magnitude of stochastic and quantum disturbances. Furthermore, we demonstrate that PBH production is feasible even when the potential exhibits a running spectral index. Finally, we assess the observational constraints on PBHs generated in this scenario.

We determine the exact distribution of the deepest vertex count in labeled ordered trees of a fixed size $n$. Specifically, we establish that the probability of the deepest vertex being at distance $k$ from the root for trees with $n$ vertices is given by the formula:
$$ \frac{2n}{n+k+1}\binom{n+k+1}{n}\binom{2n-k-1}{n-1} $$
Furthermore, we derive the corresponding bivariate generating function. Our findings also include the exact distribution for the deepest vertex in labeled ordered trees where $n$ edges are present; here, if the deepest vertex is at distance $k$ from the root for such a tree, the probability is:
$$ \frac{2n}{n+k+1}\binom{n+k+1}{n}\binom{2n-k-2}{n-1} $$
Consequently, we provide the bivariate generating function for this scenario as well.

In the 2020 United States elections, over 138 million votes were cast, with more than 60 million requiring manual tabulation due to scanner malfunctions. This surge in manual counting significantly increased the risk of human error, a concern that was amplified by the widespread misinformation regarding election fraud. To address these challenges, we introduce iOCR, a system designed to automate the counting of ballots through Optical Character Recognition (OCR). Our approach integrates multiple strategies to enhance accuracy, including the use of high-resolution images, domain-specific training data, and a novel method for correcting OCR errors by leveraging the inherent structure of ballot layouts. We evaluated iOCR on a dataset of 100,000 images from the 2020 Pennsylvania elections, demonstrating that it achieves a 99.99% accuracy rate in tallying votes for individual candidates.

This study investigates linear time series models where the parameter count exceeds the sample size, specifically examining the phenomenon of over-parameterization. In this context, "misfitting" describes a scenario where the empirical loss remains bounded away from zero even as the sample size approaches infinity. We demonstrate that, provided the over-parameterization level grows slowly relative to the sample size, the excess loss converges to zero in probability. Furthermore, we establish a central limit theorem for the excess loss, which enables the construction of confidence intervals for the true parameter vector. These theoretical results are validated through both numerical simulations and real-world data analysis.

This study examines a stochastic, multi-agent storage planning problem within a competitive electricity market, where a group of strategic generators collaborates to maximize their combined profits. These agents operate under a cautious self-planning framework, utilizing a robust Nash equilibrium to ensure profit maximization despite uncertainties in market demand and generation costs. We establish the existence of a unique, cautious self-planning outcome and develop an efficient algorithm to compute it. Furthermore, we analyze the convergence of the proposed method and investigate the relationship between this cautious self-planning solution and the standard Nash equilibrium in an idealized scenario. The research is validated through extensive numerical experiments.

This study employs a suite of zero-level cloud-top global circulation models (GCMs) to examine the atmospheric dynamics of tidally locked terrestrial planets, with a specific focus on the transition from cyclostrophic super-rotation to geostrophic turbulence. We investigate how key parameters—including planetary rotation rate, radiative timescales, and atmospheric drag—influence these circulation regimes. Our results indicate that the transition between these two regimes is governed by a single dimensionless parameter, defined as the ratio of the radiative timescale to the Rossby deformation radius squared divided by the Coriolis parameter squared. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the absolute rotation rate is not a determining factor for the circulation state; rather, the system's behavior depends on the interplay between radiative and advective timescales. Finally, we explore the impact of varying drag coefficients on the resulting atmospheric states.

Deep neural networks have become the standard for solving complex problems in computer vision, natural language processing, and other domains. Although these models often achieve high accuracy, they typically reach these results after extensive training, which is both costly and time-consuming. Furthermore, the vast amount of data required for such training limits the ability to apply these systems to real-world scenarios where data is scarce. To overcome these obstacles, this paper introduces a suite of techniques designed to accelerate learning and improve performance even with limited datasets. These methods include curriculum learning, data augmentation, and the use of transfer learning. By combining these strategies, we demonstrate that a neural network can reach ImageNet-level accuracy using only 1000 images for training.

The performance of silicon spin qubits is significantly influenced by exchange interactions between electrons trapped at donor impurities, which arise from both nuclear spins and the proximity of other donors. While the impact of nuclear spins can be effectively managed through dynamical decoupling, the influence of neighboring donors remains a critical challenge. This study employs a complete configuration interaction approach to compute exchange couplings between donor pairs in silicon, explicitly accounting for all nuclear spins and nearby donors. By applying multi-valley effective Hamiltonian theory, the calculations utilize a basis set of 1000 states, enabling the simulation of donor pairs situated up to 10 nm apart. The results indicate that the presence of other donors substantially alters the spatial dependence of the exchange interaction, a phenomenon that varies depending on the specific valley states of the system. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the exchange interaction is highly sensitive to the nuclear spin configuration of the silicon lattice. Finally, the authors present a practical strategy to mitigate the effects of neighboring donors by selecting specific donor states, thereby enhancing the fidelity of silicon spin qubits.

We present a theoretical study of quantum transport within HgTe nanostrips featuring two types of trenches: those with and without a HgTe membrane. Our analysis reveals that a trench containing a HgTe membrane functions as a highly selective filter for Dirac particles. Specifically, it allows only particles with a transverse momentum exceeding a defined threshold to traverse the structure, while reflecting those below this limit. This selectivity arises because the trench induces a tunable, negative effective mass for Dirac particles, enabling the confinement of specific transverse momentum states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transverse momentum threshold can be precisely adjusted by varying the width of the trench.

Dynamic Time Division Duplexing (TDD) allows base stations to adjust uplink and downlink time slot configurations based on current traffic demands, offering a flexible solution for asymmetric data patterns in 4G and 5G networks. However, uncoordinated decisions by base stations can lead to severe uplink interference, making the joint optimization of TDD configurations and resource allocation a critical challenge. This paper introduces a game-theoretic model allocation framework designed to optimize TDD settings while managing interference. The model defines a non-cooperative game where each base station acts as an independent player aiming to maximize its own utility. Within this framework, the utility function incorporates both the total achievable data rate and the interference generated by neighboring cells. The study analyzes the existence and uniqueness of a Nash Equilibrium and derives the specific form of the utility function to ensure convergence toward this equilibrium. Furthermore, a distributed algorithm is proposed to facilitate the calculation of the Nash Equilibrium. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the suggested algorithm effectively converges to the Nash Equilibrium and outperforms traditional static allocation methods in terms of data rate performance.

This paper introduces a novel architecture for neural networks that are constrained to specific manifolds, utilizing a symplectic integrator to ensure the preservation of these manifold constraints during forward propagation. The authors demonstrate that this approach also guarantees the preservation of specific gradient structures during backpropagation. The paper concludes by outlining the benefits of this architecture, including enhanced training stability and the ability to learn time-dependent data.

Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly deployed in critical applications, yet their widespread adoption is hindered by reliability concerns. While existing research has explored methods to boost trust in ML systems, this study focuses on enhancing the trustworthiness of the models themselves. We introduce a novel human-in-the-loop online multi-agent framework that leverages human input to improve model reliability. The proposed approach utilizes a multi-agent system where agents interact with an ML model, receive predictions, and assign trust scores to those outputs. Based on these scores, agents decide whether to accept the prediction or request human intervention for data enrichment. This enriched data is then used to update the model via online learning. We validate the framework using a real-world dataset of news articles, demonstrating that the human-in-the-loop multi-agent method significantly improves the accuracy of an initial news classifier.

We introduce a new quantum invariant defined for chains within the cylinder $T^2 \times I$, where $T^2$ represents the two-torus. This invariant is constructed to be sensitive to the geometric embedding of the chain and exhibits asymptotic behavior resembling volume constraints as the level parameter approaches infinity. Furthermore, we establish a connection between this invariant and the quantum invariants of knots and links previously developed by the authors.

Word sense disambiguation (WSD) remains a significant challenge in natural language processing, primarily due to the difficulty in distinguishing between semantically similar word senses. This paper introduces Context-Gloss Enhancement (CGE), a novel method designed to improve WSD performance. The CGE framework integrates a knowledge base enriched with context-specific definitions, allowing for more precise disambiguation by leveraging detailed semantic information. The proposed approach was evaluated using the Senseval-2 and SemEval-2007 datasets, demonstrating significant performance gains over existing state-of-the-art methods. These results indicate that providing context-aware definitions substantially enhances the accuracy of automatic word sense disambiguation.

This work introduces two novel integral representations for the reciprocal Gamma function, $1/\Gamma(z)$, utilizing the regularized incomplete gamma function, $P(a,x)$. These formulations are derived as regularized versions of the standard integral definitions for the Gamma and its incomplete variants. We demonstrate that these new expressions are mathematically equivalent to the well-known Kummer's continued fraction expansion of the Gamma function and also establish a fresh continued fraction representation.

This study examines the feasibility of identifying top quark production in proton-nucleus ($p$-A) collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) using the ALICE detector. The analysis relies on Monte Carlo simulations of $p$-A interactions generated by the EPOS 3 and EPOS LHC models, which incorporate both perturbative QCD and phenomenological approaches to describe hard scattering processes. The analysis focuses on the rapidity distribution of top quarks, utilizing the $p_T$ spectrum and the number of reconstructed top quarks as key observables. The results indicate that the EPOS LHC model provides a superior description of the data compared to EPOS 3. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that top quark generation can be successfully identified through these specific observables.

Cross-domain text-to-SQL conversion is a highly relevant yet difficult task that demands models to accurately interpret natural language queries and generate corresponding SQL statements. A primary obstacle in this area is the semantic gap between natural language and SQL, which often results in inaccurate parsing and subpar performance. To bridge this divide, we introduce a novel end-to-end cross-domain text-to-SQL framework featuring a meaningful parsing module. This module employs a cross-attention mechanism to extract key tokens from both the query and the database schema, subsequently utilizing a hierarchical decoder to reconstruct the SQL output. Furthermore, we incorporate a supportive task designed to enhance the model's ability to handle complex join operations. We evaluated our approach on three major cross-domain datasets: Spider, WikiSQL, and Spider's sub-domain, Spider's domain. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across all datasets, achieving a 0.9-point improvement in execution accuracy on the Spider dataset.

This paper introduces a novel framework for differential privacy (DP) specifically designed for graph-organized data. We define this DP variant to ensure that the disclosure of a single node's membership within a graph remains private, even when an adversary possesses full knowledge of the graph's structure and access to all other nodes' data. We argue that this approach is essential for protecting individual privacy in the context of increasingly prevalent graph-based applications. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this node-centric definition is more appropriate than the standard edge-centric DP model, which fails to provide adequate privacy guarantees when the graph topology is known to the attacker. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of our proposed definition by applying it to various real-world graph analytics tasks.

The Euclid space mission, launched in 2023, is dedicated to mapping the three-dimensional distribution of galaxies across the cosmos. By collecting extensive data on galaxy shapes, positions, and other properties, Euclid aims to investigate dark energy and dark matter through weak gravitational lensing and galaxy clustering. Complementing these primary goals, the mission offers significant opportunities for diverse ancillary research. This paper outlines the ancillary science objectives of Euclid, categorizing them into four main areas: astrophysics of galaxies, cosmology beyond the primary goals, astrophysics of the early universe, and astrophysics of the solar system. It also details the mission's data processing pipeline, the upcoming Euclid Data Archive, and the upcoming Data Release 1 (DR1). Finally, it provides an overview of the anticipated Data Release 2 (DR2) and the upcoming Euclid Symposium, which will feature presentations on the mission's ancillary science goals.

Hydrodynamic descriptions of quantum fluids are frequently hindered by the necessity of solving complex quantum kinetic equations, which can be intractable for interacting systems. This study introduces a novel hydrodynamic framework for interacting Bose fluids that relies on a classical stochastic representation of the quantum wavefunction. By averaging the classical equations of motion over this random ensemble, the approach derives a closed set of hydrodynamic equations. These equations are expressed solely in terms of the fluid's density and velocity, along with a newly defined quantity termed the "quantum stress." The resulting model is validated against exact solutions for the Bogoliubov and Gross-Pitaevskii limits. Furthermore, the framework is applied to analyze the dynamics of a quantum vortex and a quantum shock wave within a two-dimensional interacting Bose gas.

This study examines the extensive deviation behavior of the count of specific letters within words formed from sequences of related letters. We establish several novel, large-scale deviation results applicable to various sequences of letters, including those generated by deterministic processes, random walks, and Markov chains.

We demonstrate that this category possesses a well-defined metric and is complete. Furthermore, we establish the existence of region-minimizing surfaces for specific classes of closed curves. These findings are extended to the case of maps from a torus into a complete, simply connected area with non-positive curvature.

This study introduces a novel function representation designed to significantly accelerate the exact computation of Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimation and maximum likelihood (ML) within graphical models. By streamlining these core tasks, the proposed depiction facilitates faster optimization and more efficient inference across complex probabilistic structures.

Photon recoil, a phenomenon often disregarded in single-beam absorption spectroscopy, is investigated here within the context of an ultra-cold strontium vapor. We present a theoretical framework that accounts for both the recoil effect and the influence of the probe beam's intensity. This model is subsequently validated through experimental data obtained from a single-beam absorption spectroscopy setup utilizing a near-resonant probe beam directed at an ultra-cold strontium vapor cell. The findings reveal that photon recoil significantly alters the spectral line shape, inducing a red shift and broadening of the resonance. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the intensity of the probe beam plays a critical role in determining the magnitude of the recoil effect.

This study examines the transition from a shear-thinning regime to a shear-thickening regime in colloidal suspensions containing shear-thickening nanoparticles. We analyze this transition using a generalized Krieger-Dougherty (KD) framework, which incorporates a tunable parameter to account for the transition. By fitting this model to experimental data on the viscosity of cornstarch suspensions across various solid volume fractions, we determine the optimal parameter values. Furthermore, we apply the generalized KD model to predict viscosity behavior in systems with different solid volume fractions and cornstarch particle sizes. Our findings indicate that the generalized KD model effectively captures the viscosity evolution across these diverse conditions. Additionally, we observe that the shear rate required to trigger the transition scales globally with the solid volume fraction and particle diameter. Finally, we propose a theoretical explanation for this scaling behavior based on the relationship between the shear rate, solid volume fraction, and particle size.

This paper establishes that the stabilizer of the $n$-th power of the elementary symmetric polynomial within the $n$-th tensor power of the adjoint representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ is isomorphic to the Racah algebra $R_n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the associated graded algebra of the polynomial ring, graded by the Hilbert-Poincaré ordering, is isomorphic to the universal enveloping algebra of this Lie algebra. Specifically, when $n=2$, this sequence corresponds to the well-known Poincaré-Birkhoff-Witt (PBW) theorem for the $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Racah algebra $R_2$.

This study investigates the hypothesis that Google's personalized search results cause users to overlook relevant information, a phenomenon known as the "filter bubble." To test this, we conducted an experiment where participants searched for a specific topic using Google, while we recorded their mouse movements and tracked the information they viewed. The findings revealed that users frequently failed to notice content that was visible on the screen, and that personalized settings significantly increased the amount of missed information. These results demonstrate that search engine personalization can lead to a substantial loss of relevant data, even when that information is directly in the user's view.

The proposed TeV-scale muon-ion accelerator represents a novel concept for a high-energy muon collider, designed to overcome current limitations in luminosity and energy reach. This system utilizes a muon ring composed of a linear accelerator, a recirculating linear collider, and a circular booster, which together enable the production of TeV-scale muons with high intensity. The design incorporates a 100 km linear accelerator featuring 100 GeV superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerating structures, a 10 km recirculating linear collider, and a 1 km circular booster. The linear accelerator is engineered to deliver a 10 mA muon beam current, while the recirculating linear collider serves to increase the beam energy and intensity prior to injection into the circular booster. The circular booster then accelerates the beam to the multi-TeV energy range. This architecture offers a promising pathway to achieve unprecedented luminosity and center-of-mass energies, potentially reaching up to 100 TeV.

This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-adjusted 4D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (TSE) MRI technique designed for whole-body imaging. The method integrates a standard 3D TSE sequence with a motion correction module that utilizes retrospective gating based on respiratory signals. This gating system dynamically modifies the sequence's repetition time (TR) and echo time (TE) throughout the respiratory cycle to ensure consistent image quality across all respiratory phases. Specifically, the sequence parameters are optimized to capture the end-expiratory phase, which typically yields the highest image quality. The resulting 4D dataset comprises a single 3D volume acquired at end expiration and four additional 3D volumes captured at varying points within the respiratory cycle. The study details the implementation of this approach, including the specific sequence parameter configurations and the algorithm used for motion correction. Finally, the method's efficacy is demonstrated through in vivo results obtained from a healthy volunteer.

Automated metrics, such as BLEU, are standard for evaluating machine translation, yet they lack interpretability because they do not reveal which specific translation errors drive a low score. To address this, we introduce Precise Paired-Permutation Examination (PreciPe), a method that identifies the most influential word-level edit causing a significant drop in a metric. By precisely locating these critical edits, researchers can better understand the limitations of current metrics and the capabilities of translation models. We evaluate PreciPe on the WMT 2014 English-to-French and English-to-Chinese machine translation test sets, demonstrating its effectiveness in pinpointing key edits for both metrics and models.

This study introduces a comprehensive dataset covering the U.S. cargo shipping industry from 1966 to 2019, synthesizing data on new vessel construction, used sales, and scrapping values alongside historical freight rates, shipment volumes, and cost metrics. By integrating these elements, the paper offers the most extensive sectoral record available, enabling the derivation of capital stock estimates for the fleet. The authors employ these figures to construct a dynamic model of new and secondhand vessel markets, which they utilize to analyze the determinants of investment in new builds, the drivers behind used transactions, and the factors influencing scrapping decisions.

This paper introduces a novel class of piecewise linear spaces known as fabric spaces, defined by assigning edge lengths to the sides of a triangulation of a topological manifold. We establish that the associated piecewise Euclidean metric space remains geodesic provided the triangulation's dual graph is connected. Furthermore, we examine the conditions under which these metric spaces possess negative curvature, specifically analyzing the geometric constraints required for the space to be CAT(0).

This study introduces a novel framework designed to enhance stock value forecasting by integrating the BERT model with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The proposed approach utilizes BERT to extract semantic features from textual data, while the GAN component generates synthetic data to augment the training set. The effectiveness of this method was evaluated using the Shanghai Stock Exchange dataset, with results demonstrating significant improvements in prediction accuracy compared to existing techniques.

We examine the production of double Higgs bosons at TeV $e^+e^-$ colliders, focusing on how variations in BSM Higgs sector parameters influence cross-sections and kinematic distributions. We analyze the process $e^+e^- \to ZHH$ within a simplified extension of the Standard Model featuring two Higgs doublets, where the BSM Higgs mass is constrained to be below the collider's kinematic threshold. We calculate the relevant cross-sections and differential distributions for the $e^+e^- \to ZHH$ reaction, utilizing the $e^+e^- \to ZZ^* \to ZHH$ Higgs-strahlung mechanism as the dominant contribution. We also assess the impact of the BSM Higgs on the associated production channel $e^+e^- \to b\bar{b}HH$. Our findings indicate that, given the current precision achievable at TeV $e^+e^-$ machines, this setup offers exceptional sensitivity to BSM Higgs sector parameters.

This paper examines the derivation of Lagrangians for classical gravity, covering both Newtonian gravity and Einstein's General Relativity. It highlights that while the Newtonian theory admits multiple equivalent Lagrangian formulations, the unique physical content of General Relativity is captured by the Einstein-Hilbert action. Furthermore, it clarifies that the necessity of fixing a gauge to obtain well-defined equations of motion arises directly from the diffeomorphism invariance inherent in the Einstein-Hilbert action.

This study investigates the drag asymmetry experienced by cylindrical objects moving through a granular bed filled with fluid. By conducting experiments with glass beads saturated in water, we measured the drag forces acting on cylinders of varying aspect ratios as they moved at different velocities both upward and downward. Our results indicate that the degree of drag asymmetry is governed by the ratio of the object's diameter to the bed height, as well as the Reynolds number. Specifically, we observed that larger aspect ratio cylinders and higher flow velocities result in more pronounced asymmetry. Furthermore, we identified a distinct transition in the flow regime near the object, shifting from a recirculating pattern to a jet-like structure as velocity increases.

We present an analysis of elliptic and triangular flow, specifically $v_2$ and $v_3$, in Cu+Cu and Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV within the iEBE-VMD multiphase transport framework. This study focuses on the impact of initial-state fluctuations and the equation of state on these flow coefficients. Our results indicate that initial-state fluctuations are the primary driver of both $v_2$ and $v_3$, whereas the equation of state plays a secondary role. We find that the model successfully reproduces the $v_2$ and $v_3$ values observed in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}} = 200$ GeV. Furthermore, we predict that $v_2$ and $v_3$ in Cu+Cu collisions at the same energy will be approximately 10\% higher than those in Au+Au at the same centrality class.

The ATLAS collaboration at the LHC has conducted comprehensive analyses of CP violation and rare decay processes within the beauty meson sector. This work encompasses direct CP violation in neutral $B_s$ meson decays into pairs of kaons, as well as mixing-induced CP violation in $B^0_d$ and $B^0_s$ mesons decaying into $J/\psi\phi$ and $J/\psi K^+K^-$ final states. Furthermore, the group has performed initial measurements of the lepton-universality ratios for rare flavor-changing neutral current decays of beauty mesons into muons and electrons. These evaluations provide vital inputs for global fits aimed at determining the CKM matrix.

This study introduces a preconditioned GMRES solver designed for elliptic partial differential equation (PDE) problems solved using shape-preserving discretization methods. These techniques, which include discontinuous Galerkin (DG) and hybridized DG approaches, offer high-order accuracy while maintaining stability for problems involving shocks and steep gradients. However, their substantial system sizes and dense system matrices typically necessitate iterative solution strategies. We present a novel diagonal preconditioner specifically tailored for these shape-preserving discretization schemes. Our analysis demonstrates that this preconditioner effectively approximates the inverse of the system matrix's diagonal blocks, ensuring the resulting preconditioned spectrum remains tightly clustered around unity. Consequently, the solver achieves rapid convergence, often requiring only a few iterations to reach convergence, regardless of the problem's spatial dimension or mesh resolution.

Biomechanical modeling is crucial for analyzing human movement, yet it remains a significant challenge to accurately represent soft tissue behavior. This study introduces a novel non-rigid registration technique designed to align volumetric biomechanical models with surface-based medical images. The proposed approach employs a finite element model of the body, where the surface image serves as the target for deformation. To ensure the model adapts effectively to specific anatomical variations, the method optimizes both material parameters and boundary conditions by integrating surface image features into the finite element objective function. We demonstrate the efficacy of this framework through applications in breast cancer treatment planning and lower limb movement analysis.

Scene flow estimation, which involves predicting 3D motion vectors from consecutive LiDAR scans, is vital for autonomous driving. Although deep learning methods have advanced this field, they typically require massive, manually annotated datasets. To address this limitation, we introduce a self-supervised approach that trains on unannotated data using a novel adversarial metric learning framework. This method employs a discriminator network to distinguish between real and generated flow fields, optimizing a metric space where similar motions are positioned closely together. We define a new loss function based on this metric to guide the training of the flow estimator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised techniques, even when utilizing only a small subset of annotated data.

This study introduces a novel, energy-efficient approach for categorizing images using a Spiking Random Neural Network (SRNN). The SRNN is built upon a random architecture where connection weights and neuron activation thresholds are initialized randomly and remain fixed throughout training. To address the challenge of categorizing images without labeled data, we propose a method that leverages the inherent clustering capabilities of K-Means clustering. This technique groups the SRNN's output activity patterns into distinct clusters, with each cluster center serving as a prototype for a specific image category. The resulting model achieves a classification accuracy of 98.1% on the MNIST dataset, surpassing the performance of a standard Random Neural Network (RNN) trained with backpropagation. Furthermore, the proposed system demonstrates significant energy savings, consuming approximately 99.9% less power than the conventional backpropagation-based RNN.

This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of spin-polarized strange quark matter subjected to an external magnetic field and elevated temperature. By applying the MIT bag model, we derive the thermodynamic potentials for both uncharged and charged configurations. The analysis reveals that the system's stability and phase transitions are governed by the interplay between the magnetic field strength, electric charge, and temperature. Furthermore, the influence of these parameters on the equation of state is examined.

This paper introduces the concept of an "ideal pairing" within a category of cubic graphs, defined as a collection of disjoint cycles that cover every vertex and possess a specific property regarding their lengths. We establish a connection between these ideal pairings and Hamiltonian circuits, demonstrating that a cubic graph admits a Hamiltonian circuit if and only if it contains an ideal pairing where all cycles have even lengths. Furthermore, we define a new graph parameter called the "edge-tinting number," representing the minimum count of cycles required in an ideal pairing for a given graph. We investigate the characteristics of this parameter and determine its exact value for several specific classes of cubic graphs.

This study introduces Timeloops, a novel approach designed to automatically generate system call rules for containerized microservices. Timeloops operates by analyzing the system calls made by a specific service to construct a set of rules that define the allowable calls for that service. These rules are then enforced using Linux seccomp filters to restrict unauthorized activity. The primary objective of Timeloops is to mitigate the risk of container escapes by blocking illicit system calls originating from compromised services. To achieve this, the method leverages the concept of "timeloops"—recurring sequences of system calls observed within a service's execution history. By identifying these patterns, Timeloops derives rules that are both precise and adaptable, ensuring they accommodate legitimate variations in calls while filtering out malicious ones. The resulting rules are applied to the target service to enforce strict call limits. We evaluated Timeloops through two distinct experiments: first, we assessed its ability to detect known container escape attacks on real-world services, and second, we examined its performance on services with varying degrees of complexity. The results demonstrate that Timeloops successfully identifies escape attacks across all tested services and effectively handles services with diverse complexity levels.

This study introduces a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter incorporating a lattice-based constant velocity target birth model. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on approximations, this method derives the exact update equations for the intensity, cardinality distribution, and multi-Bernoulli components. The resulting intensity update is formulated as a ratio of two integrals, which are evaluated precisely using the lattice structure. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed filter achieves high accuracy in tracking while maintaining low computational costs. Furthermore, the framework is applied to optimize sensor management strategies, specifically by determining the optimal allocation of detection thresholds.

This study examines the internal null controllability of a species dynamics governed by a logistic growth term within a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ ($d \geq 1$). The system is coupled with a boundary condition that induces internal degeneracy, specifically a Dirichlet condition on a subregion $\omega \subset \Omega$. We establish that the associated adjoint system admits an observability estimate, which directly implies the internal null controllability of the species dynamics.

Soccer is a dynamic sport where strategic decisions are vital for success. This study introduces a soccer decision-making framework based on deep reinforcement learning (DRL) designed to assist players in selecting optimal moves. The proposed approach trains an agent to navigate a soccer field, make decisions, and execute actions within a simulated environment. The agent learns through trial and error to maximize goals scored while minimizing those conceded. The research details the training methodology, the design of the simulation environment, and the specific DRL algorithms employed. Furthermore, it presents an analysis of the agent's performance and its decision-making capabilities. The paper concludes with a discussion of the findings and potential future research directions.

Expanding the dimensionality of time in source inversion offers a promising avenue for mitigating the non-convex nature of the problem. However, this approach currently demands prohibitive computational resources, particularly for large-scale seismic applications. To address this bottleneck, we introduce a novel time-domain expanded source waveform inversion framework that leverages a mixed finite element method (MFEM) for spatial discretization and a time-stepping scheme for temporal evolution. By exploiting the inherent sparsity of the MFEM system matrices, we develop an efficient, scalable algorithm utilizing a time-domain expanded source alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). This strategy decomposes the high-dimensional optimization task into smaller, independent sub-problems solvable in parallel. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our time-domain expanded source ADMM approach achieves a significant reduction in computational time compared to conventional expanded source gradient-based techniques.

This study examines a spatial stochastic model of species interactions characterized by competition-colonization balance within a chaotic voter model framework. In this system, superior colonizers displace inferior ones through local displacement, while the latter compete more effectively for resources at established sites. We analyze the conditions under which inferior species are eliminated and explore the parameter regimes allowing for the stable coexistence of both species. Our findings indicate that the system exhibits a hysteresis loop, where the specific colonization advantage required for coexistence depends on the colonization advantage of the inferior species. Furthermore, we observe a distinct spatial pattern in the system's steady state, marked by the segregation of the two species.

This study investigates a device-to-device (D2D) communication system operating within an integrated data and power network, where the network utilizes an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) to facilitate power transfer to a remote load. The objective is to maximize the total data rate for both the power line communication (PLC) and D2D links by optimizing the IRS configuration, the power transmission parameters, and the D2D transmission strategy. The resulting non-convex optimization problem is addressed through successive convex approximation techniques. Numerical simulations are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

This study introduces a remote LDV configuration designed to acquire two-dimensional velocity data from a single-point LDV system. The setup employs a single-point LDV unit, a retroreflective prism, and a mirror mounted on a linear motorized stage to facilitate distant operation. Theoretical analysis and experimental results confirm that this arrangement enables the measurement of velocity vectors in two dimensions. Furthermore, the system's capabilities were successfully demonstrated by assessing the flow within a pipe.

This study introduces a programmable phase disk (PPD) designed for transmission electron microscopes (TEMs), capable of dynamically adjusting the electrostatic potential across the entire beam path. By integrating this device with a TEM, researchers can manipulate the wavefront of the electron beam, offering a novel approach to correct spherical aberration and compensate for sample-induced phase shifts. The paper details the PPD's fabrication, presents experimental data confirming its functionality, and outlines the theoretical basis for its use in correcting spherical aberration. Furthermore, it explores the potential of the PPD to enhance resolution by mitigating chromatic and spherical aberrations, as well as improving contrast through the correction of sample-related aberrations.

This paper investigates the $p$-adic regulator map for abelian extensions of non-commutative quadratic fields, which are defined as quadratic extensions of the cyclotomic field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_p)$, where $\zeta_p$ is a primitive $p$-th root of unity. The Belle II experiment at the KEKB asymmetric $e^+e^-$ collider is currently investigating a wide array of physics topics, including rare $B$ meson decay modes. This work examines the potential for detecting axion-like particles (ALPs) produced via the decay $B^0 \to K^{*0} a$, followed by the decay $K^{*0} \to K\pi$, where the resulting ALP manifests as missing momentum and displaced vertices. We determine the sensitivity of Belle II to these signatures across various ALP mass and coupling parameter spaces, specifically targeting scenarios where the ALP is either highly displaced or difficult to detect due to low ionization signals. Our analysis reveals that Belle II can probe couplings as strong as $g \sim 10^{-4} \text{ GeV}^{-1}$ for an ALP mass of $m_a = 1$ GeV. These findings offer significant constraints on models predicting ALPs with displaced or elusive characteristics.

This study introduces a novel framework designed to identify semantic shifts within sentences, a phenomenon where the meaning of a word changes based on its surrounding context. Unlike previous approaches that rely on isolated word embeddings, this contextualized language framework integrates contextual information directly into the representation of individual words. The proposed method utilizes a hybrid architecture combining a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and a Contextualized Language Framework (CLF) to generate word representations that are both context-aware and semantically robust. The CLF component specifically models the contextual nuances of words, while the RNN captures the sequential dependencies inherent in natural language. The framework was evaluated on the SemEval-2017 Task 4 dataset, which focuses on recognizing semantic alteration. Evaluation results indicate that this contextualized language framework outperforms existing methods, demonstrating superior accuracy in detecting when a word's meaning diverges from its standard usage due to contextual influences.

The detection of ultralight bosons through the spins of massive compact objects has recently emerged as a promising avenue for probing new physics. This paper investigates how the spins of massive quasar black holes can reveal the presence of ultralight bosons via the mechanism of superradiance. We demonstrate that the characteristic mass and spin of these bosons are determined by the specific quasar's mass and the surrounding environment where the black hole resides. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of identifying these bosons by analyzing the correlation between the spins and masses of quasar black holes. Our findings indicate that current and future observational data from instruments such as Chandra, NuSTAR, and eROSITA will significantly enhance the sensitivity of this detection method.

Interkinetic nuclear movement (INM) is a fundamental mechanism in neuroepithelia that directs cell proliferation and migration. While INM is well-documented in the embryonic retina, its underlying physical drivers remain unclear. Using INM in the zebrafish retina as a model system, we demonstrate that it functions as a dispersive process. We observed that nuclei migrate from the basal to the apical side at a velocity proportional to their distance from the apical surface. Furthermore, nuclei exhibit a longer residence time at the basal pole compared to the apical pole. We propose that this behavior results from a combination of basal-directed migration and a bias toward basal cell division. Our findings suggest that INM operates as a dispersive mechanism, a concept that may apply broadly to neuroepithelia.

The proposed approach leverages the inherent structural correlations within images and videos to enhance segmentation accuracy. We demonstrate that this method is applicable to a broad spectrum of demosaicing and compressive recovery algorithms. Empirical results indicate that integrating this new segmentation strategy into current algorithms yields substantial performance gains in both image and video demosaicing, as well as compressive video restoration tasks.
